title: Mexican state capitals
subtitle: All 31 states
about: The capital of each of Mexico's 31 states, ordered from the north-west to the Yucatán peninsula. Mexico City is a federal entity in its own right, not a state, so it is not included.

cards.note: Its name blends México and California, just as its twin across the border, Calexico, blends California and Mexico.
Spanish for peace; Hernán Cortés landed on its bay in 1535 and tried, unsuccessfully, to found a colony there.
Formerly the Villa del Pitic; renamed in 1828 after José María González de Hermosillo, an insurgent general in the independence war.
Miguel Hidalgo, father of Mexican independence, was imprisoned and executed here in 1811; Pancho Villa's former home is now a museum.
Founded by the Spanish in 1531 as the Villa de San Miguel; its official name, Culiacán Rosales, honours General Antonio Rosales.
Founded by conquistador Nuño de Guzmán in 1531; birthplace of the poet and diplomat Amado Nervo.
Named by Francisco de Ibarra after his Basque hometown in Spain; officially Victoria de Durango, and the backdrop to many Hollywood westerns.
Founded in 1577, it lends its name to Saltillo tile and is famous for its brightly striped woven sarapes.
Founded in 1596 and named after the Count of Monterrey, viceroy of New Spain; the saddle-shaped Cerro de la Silla dominates its skyline.
Founded in 1750 as the Villa de Santa María de Aguayo; renamed in 1825 after Guadalupe Victoria, Mexico's first president.
Named after Saint Louis, King of France, and the rich silver mines of Potosí in Bolivia, echoing the mines that prompted its founding.
A silver mining city founded in 1548, with a UNESCO-listed centre; Pancho Villa's forces captured it in the Battle of Zacatecas in 1914.
Its name means hot waters, after the local thermal springs; it hosts the vast Feria Nacional de San Marcos every spring.
Named after Guadalajara in Spain, birthplace of conquistador Nuño de Guzmán; the city is strongly associated with mariachi and tequila.
Founded by the Spanish in 1523 and moved to its present site in 1527; it lies near the active Volcán de Colima.
Called Valladolid until 1828, when it was renamed after José María Morelos, the independence hero born there; its centre is UNESCO listed.
The first battle of the independence war was fought at its Alhóndiga de Granaditas granary in 1810; birthplace of muralist Diego Rivera.
Emperor Maximilian was executed on its Cerro de las Campanas in 1867, and Mexico's 1917 Constitution was drafted here. Officially Santiago de Querétaro.
Cornish miners brought football and pastes, a local pasty, to this mining town; strong winds earn it the nickname La Bella Airosa.
Its name probably means place of maize bread in Nahuatl; the Tlaxcalans allied with Hernán Cortés against the Aztecs.
Mexican forces defeated the French army here on 5 May 1862, the origin of Cinco de Mayo; also the home of mole poblano.
Long famed for its chorizo sausage; it sits beneath the Nevado de Toluca, a volcano whose crater holds two lakes reachable by car.
Its name is a Spanish rendering of the Nahuatl Cuauhnāhuac, near the trees; Humboldt nicknamed it the City of Eternal Spring.
Morelos convened the Congress of Chilpancingo here in 1813, which declared independence from Spain; the name means place of wasps in Nahuatl.
Officially Oaxaca de Juárez after Benito Juárez, a native of the state; its centre and nearby Monte Albán form a joint UNESCO site.
The jalapeño pepper is named after the city, also spelled Jalapa; its university earns it the nickname Athens of Veracruz.
Its name means beautiful town; the Parque-Museo La Venta holds a celebrated collection of Olmec artefacts, including colossal stone heads.
Tuxtla comes from Nahuatl for place of rabbits; Gutiérrez honours Joaquín Miguel Gutiérrez, a governor who promoted Chiapas joining Mexico.
Officially San Francisco de Campeche; its walls and bastions, built between 1686 and 1704 to repel pirates, are UNESCO listed.
Built in 1542 on the Maya city of Ti'ho, reusing its carved stones; nicknamed the White City for its white limestone facades.
Founded in 1898 as Payo Obispo on Chetumal Bay, near the mouth of the Río Hondo on the border with Belize; renamed in 1936.
